sentences.text: In view of the present legal position as held by our Hon'ble High Court as well as Apex Court of India in a catena of decisions as well as relevant provisions of the Act, this court has to see whether the complainant has complied all the requirements as contained in Sec.138 of NI Act so as to bring home the guilt of the accused for the alleged offence.
If so, whether the accused is able to rebut the legal presumption available to the complainant under Sec.139 of the Act by adducing probable defense or not.

However, it is held by the full bench of our Apex Court in the case of Rangappa Vs. Mohan reported in 2010 (1) DCR 706 that;
"The Statutory presumption man- dated by sec.139 of the Act, does in- deed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability.

entities.text: Rangappa Vs. Mohan reported in 2010 (1) DCR 706
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, the presumption U/S 139 of the Act is in the nature of a rebuttable pre- sumption and it is open for the ac- cused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested".

10. Therefore, in view of the above decision, once the cheque is admitted, the statutory presumption would automatically fall in favour of the complainant that, the alleged cheque was issued for discharge of an existing legally enforceable debt or liability against the accused and the burden will shift on to the accused to rebut the same.
INGREDIENTS OF OFFENCE AND DISCUSSION:-
11.
Before dwelling into the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides.
In order to establish the offence under Section 138 of NI Act, the prosecution must fulfill all the essential ingredients of the offence.

A demand of the said amount has been made by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque by a notice in writing given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information of the dishonour of cheque from the bank;

The accused can only be held guilty of the offence under Section 138 NI Act if the above-mentioned ingredients are proved by the complainant co-extensively.
Additionally, the conditions stipulated under Section 142 NI Act have to be fulfilled.
Notably, there is no dispute at bar about the proof of only first, third, and fifth ingredient.
The complainant had proved the original cheques vide Ex.P.1 to 6 which the accused person had not disputed as being drawn on the account of the accused.
It was not disputed that the cheques in question was presented within its validity period.
The cheques in question was returned unpaid vide return memo dated 29.09.2022 vide Ex.P.7 to 12 due to the reason, "Exceeds Arrangment".
The complainant had proved the service of legal demand notice dated 06.10.2022 vide Ex.P.13 by bringing on record the postal receipt vide Ex.P.14, Ex-P15-postal cover, Ex
. P16 to 21 are the Tax Invoices, Ex.P22 is the E-way bill and Ex.P23 is the Ledger Account.
Thus, there is a dispute only with regard to the second ingredient to the offence.
As such, the 1 st,3rd,4th& 5th ingredient of the offence under section 138 of the NI Act stands proved.
13. As far as the proof of second ingredient is concerned, the complainant has to prove that the cheque in question was drawn by the drawer for discharging a legally enforceable debtor any liability.
In the present case, the issuance of the cheque in question is not denied.
As per the scheme of the NI Act, once the accused admits signature on the cheque in question, certain presumption are drawn, which result in shifting of onus.
Section 118(a) of the NI Act lays down the presumption that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration.
Another presumption is enumerated in Section 139 of NI Act.
The provision lays down the presumption that the holder of the cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or part, of any debt or other liability.
14. The combined effect of these two provisions is a presumption that the cheque is drawn for consideration and given by the accused for the discharge of debt or other liability.
Both the sections use the expression "shall", which makes it imperative for the court to raise the presumptions once the foundational facts required for the same are proved.

Reliance is placed upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, Hiten P. Dalal vs. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001) 6 SCC 16.
15.

Once the presumption is raised, it is for the accused to rebut the same by establishing a probable defence.
16. The presumptions raised under Section 118(b) and Section 139 NI Act are rebuttable presumptions.

A reverse onus is cast on the accused, who has to establish a probable defence on the standard of preponderance of probabilities to prove that either there was no legally enforceable debt or other liability.

sentences.text: On perusal of cross-examination of PW-1, accused counsel has not disputed business relationship and transaction between complainant and him.

Even accused has not disputed the issuance of cheque and signature of accused in cheque, accused counsel only taken contention/defence that goods alleged to be supplied as per the tax invoice Ex- P16 to 22 based on which complainant claiming amount as due is not at all delivered to him.
18. That goods has not been delivered to him as per Ex- P16 to 22 invoices and hence there is no liability and no question of issuance of cheque for discharging of due arises.

Further argued that Ex-P16 to 22 are tax invoices are preparedand generated by PW-1 in his office only and ledger account Ex-P23 also prepared by PW-1 and hence Ex-P16 to 23 are not believable and acceptable.
Further argued that cheque in question was issued by accused to PW-1 at commencement of business as security and has been misused by PW-1 and filed this false case.

19. In this regard on perusal of the cross-examination of the PW-1, accused has taken the contention that the goods mentioned in the invoice Ex-P16 to 22 has not delivered to him for which PW-1 has clearly denied the same.

Further with regard to the specific question that delivery challan has not been produced, PW-1 stated that delivery challan will be given to the recipient and luggage receipt will be given to them and he will produce the same.
Further PW-1 has clarified that since it was the inter state transport, there will be no delivery challans only luggage receipt will be given.

20. In support of his contention, complainant has produced the tax invoice as per Ex-P16 to 22 which clearly shows that various goods mentioned in Ex-P16 to 22 worth of Rs.2,11,869/- and Rs.1,70,054/- and Rs.2,06,562/-, Rs.2,15,905/- Rs.2,11,720=07 has been transported from the complainant company to the accused company.
Though accused contended that they are printed out from the complainant's office and the goods were not delivered to him.
But in order to prove his defence, accused has not examined himself and also produced any single document to show that the goods as per ex-P16 to 22 are not delivered to his office or company.
Moreover complainant has produced E-ways bills attached with the Ex-P16 to 22 which are generated from the government website.
Generally E-ways bills will be generated only with the tax on goods are paid and transported.
Even the E-ways bill clearly shows that the goods worth of cheque amount has been transported to the accused company Sri.Wall stickers on the specific date.
Even the EV bills cannot be prepared by the complainant, there is a presumption with regard to the government website generated bills from the website to be as genuine and authenticated.
Even the ledger statement Ex-P23 clearly shows that accused was due of the cheque amount towards the PW-1 in respect of the goods transported to him as per Ex-P16 to 22.
Accused being carrying on the business, certainly would have maintained the ledger statement and the account statement.

If at all accused has not received the goods transported as per Ex-P16 to 22, certainly the same would be reflected in the account statement or the ledger statement and he could have produce the same to prove his contention.
But accused has neither stepped into the witness box nor proved his defence by producing an cogent and reliable evidence.
On the other hand, complainant has clearly established that he has supplied the goods as per Ex-P16 to 22 and accused is due of the cheque amount.
Ex- P23 ledger statement clearly shows accused is due of amount and has issued cheques in question towards the said due amount.

sentences.text: Further though accused contended that the cheques in question were issued as a security during the commencement of the business with the complainant, but accused has failed to prove that there was no dues liable to be payable by him to the complainant.

Hence even though the cheques in question were issued as a security but accused has failed to prove that he is not due to the complainant any amount, the said defence cannot be believable and acceptable.
In this regard, it has been held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Sudir Kumar Bhalla Vs Jagdish Chand 2008 7 SCC 137-

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The legal position has been clarified in Sudhir Kumar Balla wherein it is made clear that criminal liability of the drawer under the provision of Sec.138 of NI Act attracted only account of dishonour of cheques issued in discharge of liability or debt but not on account of issuance of security charges of courts it cannot be laid down that as a general proposition of law that dishonour of cheque given as a security cannot attract Section 138 of NI Act.

22. Conclusion: In view of all the above discussions, it can be concluded that the complainant has established through cogent and convincing evidence the fact of issuance of the cheque for discharge of legality enforceable debt, which is dishonored for want of sufficient funds, Issuance of legal notice within stipulated time, failure on the part of accused to repay the amount within stipulated period.
On the other hand, the accused has failed to rebut the presumption available to the complainant through probable evidences that would preponderate upon the evidence lead by the complainant.
Therefore, the accused is held to have committed an offence punishable under Sec. 138 of N.I. Act.
Accordingly, Point No.1 is answered in the Affirmative.

23. POINT NO.2:- In view of my answer to point No.1, I proceed to pass the following:-
-: O R D E R :-
Acting U/Sec.278(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, accused is hereby convicted for the offence punishable U/Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
Accused is sentenced to pay a fine of Rs.12,32,986/- for the offence punishable under section 138 of N.I.Act.
The amount of Rs.12,27,986/- shall be paid to the complainant by way of compensation in accordance with Sec.395 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, within three months from today.
The remaining amount of Rs.5,000/- shall be confiscated to the state.
In default of payment of fine, the accused shall undergo simple imprisonment for a period of six months.
The bail and surety bond of the accused and surety shall stand canceled.
